evals.prompt: I'm the compliance coordinator at Oak Hollow Housing Corp, a nonprofit that owns Brookside Apartments in Raleigh — 84 units, LIHTC (year 6 of compliance) with 9 HOME-designated units. The North Carolina HFA notified us of an on-site monitoring review in about 7 weeks. Last review we had findings for two late recerts and a utility allowance that wasn't updated. Our long-time compliance person left in the spring. Give me a prep plan.
evals.expected_output: A week-by-week monitoring-visit preparation plan starting with the agency instrument and prior findings, a file-readiness checklist on the likely sample, rent roll and gross-rent reconciliation, over-income tracking, mock NSPIRE inspection, binder assembly, staff briefing, day-of conduct, and a root-cause corrective action plan, with a layered HOME matrix and attorney/CPA review.
assertions: Sequences prep backward from the visit, starting with obtaining the agency's monitoring instrument and confirming evidence that last cycle's corrective actions (late recerts, utility allowance) are in place
Runs a file-readiness checklist on the likely sample (all move-ins since the last review, flagged files, plus a random share) with columns for evidence, pass/fail, fix date, and owner
Reconciles the rent roll so every unit's gross rent (rent + mandatory fees + current utility allowance) is at or below the current limit, and checks over-income/next-available-unit tracking
Addresses the layered HOME units with a unit-by-unit program matrix applying the strictest rule per dimension

Specifies that corrective action plans should include root cause and a durable control (e.g., a recert tickler), not just single-file fixes, and that staff turnover requires systems that survive the person
Recommends attorney or CPA review of filings/responses before submission

evals.prompt: lihtc q: we charge $25/mo mandatory 'amenity fee' and a $35 pet fee (only if you have a pet) and $15 for optional storage. 2BR 60% unit, rent $1,050, UA $142. does any of that count toward gross rent?
evals.expected_output: Explains gross rent as rent plus mandatory charges plus utility allowance: the mandatory amenity fee counts, optional storage does not, and a pet fee counts only if mandatory as a condition of occupancy; computes gross rent and says to compare to the HFA's published rent limit table, noting that even small overages are noncompliance.
assertions: Defines gross rent as rent charged plus mandatory charges plus the utility allowance
Counts the mandatory amenity fee in gross rent and excludes the optional storage charge
Treats the pet fee according to whether it is a mandatory condition of occupancy rather than an optional choice
Computes gross rent of at least $1,217 ($1,050 + $25 + $142) and says to compare it to the HFA's published 2BR 60% rent limit rather than computing the limit independently
Warns that even a few dollars over the limit makes the unit noncompliant and that refunds/prospective adjustment would be required

evals.prompt: At recert, one of our tenants in a 2BR LIHTC unit (60% set-aside, Milwaukee) now makes about 160% of the current income limit — she got a big promotion. Our property manager wants to either raise her rent to market or give her notice, and in the meantime rent the next 2BR that opens up to a market-rate applicant since 'we're already over our set-aside anyway.' Is that right?
evals.expected_output: Explains the over-income (140%) rule: the tenant is over-income but not out of compliance, so no eviction or rent above the limit; the next available unit rule requires the next comparable or smaller vacant unit to go to a qualified household, otherwise the original unit permanently loses qualified status; recommends tracking and staff training, with professional review.
assertions: States that a household exceeding 140% of the current limit at recert is over-income but not out of compliance, and should not be evicted or charged rent above the limit
Explains the next available unit rule: the next comparable or smaller vacant unit must be rented to a qualified low-income household at a restricted rent
Warns that renting a comparable or larger unit to a non-qualifying household first causes the original unit to permanently lose qualified status
Rejects or challenges the 'already over our set-aside' reasoning, noting the set-aside is tested continuously at the building level and each unit's qualified status matters
Recommends flagging over-income households in the rent roll, maintaining a next-available-unit log, and training leasing staff
